summary: The note surveys child labour across history and regions, including Brazil, Europe, China, India, Australia, Africa, Iowa and Switzerland. It explains how cultural beliefs have rationalised the practice and describes its dangers in mining, glassmaking, meatpacking and agriculture. It also covers legal exceptions, corporate accusations, and difficulties in obtaining accurate present-day data.
one_line: A survey of child labour across history and world regions, covering its causes, dangerous industries, legal exceptions and corporate and government responses.
key_facts: Child labour has been a consistent struggle for children in Brazil since the country was colonized on April 22, 1550 by Pedro Álvares Cabral.
Armando Dias died in November 1913 from an electric shock when entering the textile industry where he worked.
Under EU Directive 94/33/EC, agreed by member countries in 1996, children above the age of 13 may perform light work for a limited number of hours per week.
A recent study showed over a third of Dutch twelve-year-old kids had a job, the most common being babysitting.
The overall extent of child labour in China is unclear because the government categorizes child labour data as "highly secret".
In 2014 the U.S. Department of Labor's List of Goods Produced by Child Labor or Forced Labor attributed 12 goods to China, including electronics, garments, toys and coal.
In 2012 the BBC accused Glencore of using child labour in its mining and smelting operations of Africa, and Glencore denied it.
India contributes one-third of Asia's child labour and one-fourth of the world's child labour, according to research by Indian social scientists and NGOs.
Agriprocessors, a kosher meatpacking company in Postville, employed 57 minors, some as young as 14, in violation of state law; its CEO was found not guilty of all 57 charges on 7 June 2010.
In the 1930s, 20% of all agricultural labourers in the Canton of Bern were children below the age of 15.
Swiss historian Marco Leuenberger found that in 1930 there were some 35,000 indentured children, and between 1920 and 1970 more than 100,000 were placed with families or homes.
An African NGO report claimed 80,000 child labourers under the age of 15, or about 40% of all miners, were supplying ore to Chinese companies in Congo.
Between 20,000 and 40,000 children work in artisanal mining in Mali, the third largest exporter of gold in Africa.
Human Rights Watch estimates that about 12 percent of global gold production comes from artisanal mines.
The Harkin-Engel Protocol, a voluntary agreement accepted in 2001 by the international cocoa and chocolate industry, aims to eliminate the worst forms of child labour in West Africa.
